title: Levy (2009): True or False
instructions: Evaluate the scope and strength of each claim using the article, then choose True or False.

items.prompt: Stereotype embodiment theory holds that aging is partly a social construct.
items.explanation: Levy does not deny biological aging. She argues that culturally acquired age stereotypes can also influence functioning and health.

items.prompt: In the Ohio longitudinal studies, more positive self-perceptions of aging were associated with better functional health and an average survival advantage of 7.5 years.
items.explanation: Participants were at least 50 at baseline and were followed for more than two decades. The advantages remained after adjustment for baseline functional health and other relevant variables.

items.prompt: According to the theory, people first begin learning age stereotypes in old age.
items.explanation: Children encounter age stereotypes through their environment and media. Internalization continues across the life span.

items.prompt: The 7.5-year survival difference experimentally proves that positive thinking adds exactly 7.5 years to every individual's life.
items.explanation: This was an average difference between groups in longitudinal observational data, not an experimentally established benefit guaranteed to each individual.

items.prompt: Negative age stereotypes may give young adults short-term advantages, such as priority in the allocation of limited resources.
items.explanation: Levy explains that stereotypes can justify discrimination that gives younger adults priority when limited resources are allocated.

items.prompt: Among the participants aged 18–39 at baseline, those with more negative age stereotypes were half as likely as the positive-stereotype group to experience a cardiovascular event after age 60.
items.explanation: The direction is reversed: the negative-stereotype group was twice as likely to experience a cardiovascular event after age 60, after adjustment for relevant covariates.

items.prompt: The subliminal priming procedure presented words for 55 milliseconds, allowing encoding while preventing conscious perception for most people.
items.explanation: Levy describes 55 milliseconds as fast enough to prevent conscious perception for most individuals but slow enough to permit encoding.

items.prompt: Self-relevance means that age stereotypes acquire personal resonance as old age becomes part of a person's current identity.
items.explanation: When people recognize old age as their present state rather than a remote prospect, general age stereotypes become connected to their own identity.

items.prompt: Participants exposed to positive age stereotypes tended to reject costly life-prolonging interventions more often than participants exposed to negative stereotypes.
items.explanation: The positive-stereotype group tended to accept the intervention; the negative-stereotype group tended to reject it.

items.prompt: The stereotype-matching effect refers to stronger effects when stereotype content corresponds to the domain of the outcome.
items.explanation: Effects were greatest when cognitive stereotypes corresponded to cognitive tasks or physical stereotypes corresponded to physical tasks.

items.prompt: Younger participants following the same priming protocol always showed stronger stereotype-congruent effects than older participants.
items.explanation: Younger participants tended to show no effects or much weaker effects. Levy partly explains the older participants' responses through activation of an older-person identity.

items.prompt: Subliminal exposure to negative age stereotypes reduced cardiovascular responses to stress.
items.explanation: Negative priming heightened cardiovascular stress responses, whereas positive priming reduced them.

items.prompt: The behavioral pathway includes the possibility that negative stereotypes make healthy practices seem futile and undermine self-efficacy.
items.explanation: If health problems are seen as inevitable consequences of aging, people may regard healthy practices as pointless and feel less able to influence their health.

items.prompt: Levy identifies sustained activation of positive age stereotypes in everyday life as a remaining intervention challenge.
items.explanation: Laboratory priming demonstrated potential benefits, but maintaining positive activation in everyday life remained an open challenge.

items.prompt: The article concludes that all four premises of stereotype embodiment apply unchanged to every stigmatized group.
items.explanation: Levy explicitly avoids this universal claim. The transferability of stereotype embodiment to other targeted groups remains a question for future research.
